sources.title: Motus: A Unified Latent Action World Model

sectionsRead: Abstract; Sections 1–3: introduction, related works and problem formulation (PDF pp. 1–4)
Sections 4.1–4.3: architecture, latent actions, training and data (PDF pp. 4–6)
Sections 5.1–5.4: baselines, simulation, real-world evaluation and ablation (PDF pp. 6–8)
Embedded Supplementary Material, Sections 7.1–7.2: training algorithms, five inference modes and experiments (PDF pp. 13–14; supplement pp. 1–2)
Sections 8.1–8.3 and 9.1–9.3: additional benchmarks, execution results, architecture, datasets and configuration (PDF pp. 15–19; supplement pp. 3–7)
omissions: Text extraction does not reconstruct figure images; inspect the retained PDF for figures and equation/table layout.
Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.
The extraction limitation was addressed by inspecting original PDF figures and tables. All seven text chunks were read individually, covering all 22 pages.

Identity: PDF p. 1 identifies arXiv:2512.13030v2, dated 25 December 2025. Title and all 16 authors match the catalog. The catalog labels the work CVPR 2026; no venue edition was supplied or compared, and equivalence to that edition is unverified.
The embedded ten-page Supplementary Material was read completely. Availability of any separate supplemental files remains unverified.
Code, project website and external datasets were not inspected; no experiments were reproduced. Reference-only PDF pp. 10–12 were read as text, not visually inspected.

synopsis: Motus connects video, action and understanding experts through shared attention, then uses separate modality noise levels to switch among five prediction modes. Optical-flow latent actions provide pretraining targets for videos without robot action labels. Execution results favor the complete recipe on average, but do not establish uniform generalization or isolate every architectural contribution.

problem.text: Robot policies need language understanding, visual dynamics and executable controls, yet heterogeneous videos lack compatible action labels. Motus addresses both unified prediction and cross-embodiment motion transfer. Its manipulation formulation predicts action chunks from the current image and instruction, optionally proprioception.

contributions.text: A Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) network preserves expert-specific transformations while exchanging features through Tri-model Joint Attention. Separate video/action noise levels enable conditional, marginal and joint generation.
A flow-reconstruction bottleneck with weak action supervision enables a three-stage training recipe spanning six data levels, from inherited web priors to target-robot demonstrations.

inputs: Current visual observation and language instruction; optional proprioception in the policy formulation
Noised future video/action tokens and separate flow timesteps; clean future actions or observations when required by the selected mode
outputs: Future video observations and/or latent-action or embodiment-specific action chunks, depending on training stage and inference mode

steps.name: Fuse complementary experts
steps.detail: Wan 2.2 5B supplies video priors. Frozen Qwen3-VL-2B features feed a separate understanding expert. Each branch keeps its own Transformer transformations, with shared attention connecting video, action and understanding tokens. Video and action branches receive independent flow timesteps.

steps.name: Compress visual motion
steps.detail: DPFlow produces inter-frame optical flow represented as RGB. Section 4.2 specifies DC-AE compression to four 512-dimensional tokens, followed by a 14-dimensional latent. Reconstruction, action alignment and KL regularization shape this motion target; its dimensionality alone does not guarantee executable control.

steps.name: Predict dense actions with sparse video
steps.detail: Table 11 lists eight frames at 5 Hz and 48 actions at 30 Hz, reducing redundant video tokens. The RoboTwin IDM experiment instead states a 16-action chunk; these configurations must remain distinct.

training.text: Latent-action learning mixes 90% unlabeled data with 10% labeled trajectories, including task-agnostic Curobo image/action pairs. Stage 1 adapts only the VGM; Stage 2 trains all three experts on latent actions while freezing the upstream VLM; Stage 3 specializes Motus on target-robot controls. Web priors enter through off-the-shelf models.

The model learns two rectified-flow velocity fields from independently noised video/action targets. Training data include Egodex, Agibot, RDT, RoboMind, RoboTwin, task-agnostic and in-house data. Table 13 specifies batch size 256, AdamW and approximately 8,000/10,000/400 GPU-hours across stages.

inference.text: VGM denoises video while keeping future actions noisy; VLA denoises actions while keeping future video noisy. World-model mode fixes clean actions; IDM fixes clean future observations. Joint mode denoises both streams. Algorithms 2–6 specify these modes; the joint-mode prose incorrectly points to Algorithm 2.

Table 11 lists ten inference steps. Target-robot training produces control chunks, and Figure 8 depicts execution; video prediction alone does not establish task completion. The source omits measured control latency and a complete feedback/replanning cadence.

equations.explanation: Equation (2) combines flow reconstruction, alignment between real and predicted actions, and latent-space KL regularization. Table 11 sets the alignment weight to 1.0 and KL weight to 10^{-6}.

The action velocity field is trained toward Gaussian noise minus the clean action chunk; observations use an analogous loss. Here t is observation time, k the chunk horizon and theta the learned parameters. The expectation includes examples, noise and the action flow timestep.

results.setting: 50 tasks; 2,500 clean plus 25,000 randomized demonstrations; 40k fine-tuning steps; 100 execution trials per task.
results.interpretation: Calculated randomized gains are 14.18 and 43.18 percentage points. The prose claim of over 45 points over π0.5 in randomized scenes conflicts with these means; the clean gain is 45.68 points. Uncertainty is unreported.

results.setting: RoboTwin 2.0, with downstream training after each pretraining variant.
results.value: Randomized: 77.00 without pretraining; 81.86 Stage 1; 87.02 complete recipe.
results.comparison: Full versus Stage 1: +5.16 percentage points; versus no pretraining: +10.02.
results.interpretation: Supports the combined recipe, without isolating flow supervision, architecture, data diversity or extra compute. Clean means conflict across displays.

results.setting: AC-One and Agilex-Aloha-2; 100 training trajectories per task; one multi-task model per platform.
results.interpretation: Subgoal credit is not binary success. These are printed averages; baseline reporting conflicts and omitted supplementary cube tasks limit their interpretation.

results.task: Get Water from Water Dispenser on Agilex-Aloha-2
results.setting: Table 5: ten trials per method, with subgoal weights 0, 0.4, 0.8 and 1.0.
results.interpretation: Evidence of executed task progress in a small, task-specific evaluation.

results.comparison: Joint gains 3.12 percentage points, calculated from the reported values.
results.interpretation: Favors joint inference in this setting; no latency comparison or uncertainty is reported.

results.setting: Both real-world platforms; Table 6 average row.
results.comparison: No competing world-model baseline is listed.
results.interpretation: Fidelity metrics concern predicted video, not task success. Sample count and detailed split protocol are unspecified.
Input parity is unclear: Algorithm 4 uses future observations, but the baseline description specifies current observation.

results.setting: Ten long-horizon tasks; stated standard evaluation protocol.
results.interpretation: A reported tie; fine-tuning and uncertainty details are limited.

results.setting: Three tasks, In Distribution and Cross Category tracks; π0.5 values sourced from its official implementation.
results.interpretation: Average gains coexist with lower Select Fruit scores in both tracks.

results.setting: Cube placed outside training space; supplementary Tables 15–16.
results.interpretation: Generalization varies by embodiment; Table 3 omits the Agilex cube results.

limitations.text: Figure 6/Table 14 show clean no-pretraining/Stage-1 means 77.56/82.26; Table 2 prints 72.8/82.86. Table 3 gives AC-One cube baseline 46, whereas Table 15 gives 57.5. These conflicts remain unresolved.

Improvement across all real-world tasks is not supported: Agilex oven scores are 34 versus 36 for π0.5, and its OOD cube results also favor that baseline. Stage ablations combine several changes and report no seed variability.

The authors identify more universal motion priors and learning latent actions from internet-scale general videos as future work. Inherited web priors should not be equated with demonstrated direct latent-action training on arbitrary internet video.

reproduction.text: Reproduction needs the named foundation models, DPFlow/DC-AE processing, Table 12 datasets and target-robot demonstrations. Table 13 gives GPU-hours but omits GPU model/count and software versions; exact data-mixture weights and the full execution configuration are absent.

Resolve uniform timestep sampling in Section 4.1/Algorithm 1 versus Table 11’s Logit Normal entry, and the 16-action RoboTwin description versus the 48-action configuration. Figure 3 draws five token boxes while its text specifies four; the intended implementation requires clarification.

reasoning.text: Joint prediction is supported by shared tri-expert attention and simultaneous video/action denoising. The Dual-system label is questionable: Figure 1 and Section 4.1 describe a unified MoT network with layer-level interaction, not a separately executed world-model/controller cascade. Expert-specific parameters alone do not settle that taxonomy. This reader assessment preserves the recorded classification.

discussionQuestions: Would joint inference retain its advantage with matched control latency and identical evaluation seeds? (e08, e10, e16)
How much of Stage 2’s gain comes from action alignment rather than extra heterogeneous data and compute? (e04, e12, e17)

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title/author block and arXiv margin
evidence.detail: Observed title is Motus: A Unified Latent Action World Model; all sixteen authors match the catalog. The artifact is arXiv:2512.13030v2, 25 December 2025; affiliations include Tsinghua University, Peking University and Horizon Robotics.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, Section 3, Embodied Policies, Eq. (1) and Challenges 1–2
evidence.detail: Defines observations, instructions, proprioception, actions and action chunks; motivates unified distributions and learning across heterogeneous action spaces.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Figure 1; pp. 4–5, Section 4.1, Model Architecture, Action-Dense Video-Sparse Prediction and Experts Details
evidence.detail: Tri-model Joint Attention connects separately parameterized video, action and understanding Transformers. Wan 2.2 5B and Qwen3-VL-2B provide pretrained priors. Figure 1 marks the upstream VLM frozen and feeds video/action flow timesteps into their respective AdaLN blocks. Video sampling is sparser than action sampling.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 4.2, Figure 3 and Eq. (2)
evidence.detail: DPFlow RGB flow is compressed to four 512-dimensional tokens and a 14-dimensional latent. Training combines reconstruction, action alignment and KL with 90% unlabeled and 10% labeled data, including task-agnostic Curobo supervision. Figure 3 depicts five token boxes, unlike the stated four.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 4.3, Table 1 and Figure 4
evidence.detail: Three stages adapt the VGM, train Motus experts with latent actions and frozen VLM, then fine-tune on target-robot controls. Six data levels distinguish inherited web priors from human, synthetic, task-agnostic, multi-robot and target-robot data.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 4.1, unnumbered rectified-flow losses
evidence.detail: Action and observation losses regress velocity toward Gaussian noise minus clean future targets, using separate uniformly sampled timesteps; total loss is their sum.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13 (supplement p. 1), Section 7.1, Algorithms 1–4
evidence.detail: Training noises modalities independently. VGM keeps actions noisy, world-model mode conditions on clean actions, and IDM conditions on clean current/future observations. Algorithm 1 uses discrete uniform timesteps in interpolation expressions without explicit normalization details.

evidence.location: PDF p. 14 (supplement p. 2), Section 7.1, Algorithms 5–6
evidence.detail: VLA keeps future observations noisy while denoising actions; joint mode denoises both. The joint-mode prose cites Algorithm 2 although Algorithm 6 gives the joint procedure.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 5.2 and Table 2, Average row
evidence.detail: The 50-task protocol uses 2,500 clean and 25,000 randomized demonstrations, 40k fine-tuning steps and 100 execution trials per task. Randomization covers backgrounds, clutter, table height and lighting. Table 2 prints clean no-pretraining/Stage-1 means 72.8/82.86; prose claims over 45 points over π0.5 in randomized scenes.

evidence.location: PDF p. 14 (supplement p. 2), Section 7.2, Tables 6–8 and IDM paragraph
evidence.detail: Table 6 reports two-platform world-model fidelity without a competitor. Table 7 reports MSE 0.044/0.122/0.014 over 100 samples; baseline text specifies current observations and 16-action chunks. Table 8 reports VLA 83.90 and joint 87.02 success.

evidence.location: PDF p. 18 (supplement p. 6), Table 14, full task rows and Average row
evidence.detail: Motus clean/randomized means are 88.66/87.02, X-VLA 72.8/72.84 and π0.5 42.98/43.84. No-pretraining means are 77.56/77.00 and Stage 1 means 82.26/81.86. Task rows show exceptions to Motus superiority.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Section 5.4 and Figure 6
evidence.detail: Randomized bars are 77.00, 81.86, 87.02; clean bars are 77.56, 82.26, 88.66. Arrows show differences 10.02 and 11.10 with percent signs. Variants change pretraining stages; the plot has no error bars.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–8, Section 5.3 and Table 3, task and Average rows
evidence.detail: Real-world models train jointly per platform with 100 trajectories per task and use subgoal-weighted partial success. Table 3 gives Motus means 63.22/59.30, π0.5 14.79/48.60, and no-pretraining 25.86/26.60. Agilex oven is 34 versus 36; AC-One cube baseline is printed as 46.

evidence.location: PDF p. 19 (supplement p. 7), Tables 15–16, Grab Cube, OOD, towel and oven rows
evidence.detail: Table 15 prints AC-One cube baseline 57.5. OOD cubes are outside the training space: Motus/π0.5 are 75/28.125 on AC-One and 31.25/68.75 on Agilex. Table 16 contains Agilex cube results absent from Table 3. Towel rows distinguish partial folds from full completion.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table 5, subgoal counts and Partial Success Rate row
evidence.detail: Agilex dispenser weights are 0/0.4/0.8/1.0. Motus has two 0.8 outcomes and eight full successes; π0.5 has five 0.4, four 0.8 and one full success, producing partial scores 96% and 62%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 16 (supplement p. 4), Table 11 and Section 9.1
evidence.detail: Table 11 lists 30-layer action/understanding experts, eight frames at 5 Hz, 48 actions at 30 Hz, ten inference steps, Logit Normal sampling, alignment weight 1.0, KL weight 10^{-6} and total scale 8B. No measured latency or complete feedback policy is provided.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17 (supplement p. 5), Tables 12–13
evidence.detail: Table 12 lists Egodex 230,949; Agibot 728,209; RDT 6,083; RoboMind Franka 9,589 and Aloha 7,272; RoboTwin 27,500; task-agnostic 1,000; in-house 2,000. Stage batches are 256 with AdamW, weight decay 0.01, learning rates 8e-5/5e-5/(1–5)e-5 and approximately 8,000/10,000/400 GPU-hours. Hardware models/counts and software versions are omitted.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 15–16 (supplement pp. 3–4), Section 8.2 and Tables 9–10
evidence.detail: LIBERO-Long has ten tasks; Motus and X-VLA score 97.6, OpenVLA-OFT 94.5. VLABench tests three tasks; average Motus/π0.5 fractions are 0.48/0.43 in distribution and 0.25/0.22 cross category. Select Fruit favors π0.5 in both tracks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 16, Figure 8; p. 22 (supplement p. 10), Figure 12 and caption
evidence.detail: Figure 8 is labeled real-world execution demonstrations. Figure 12 presents joint-mode real-world inference as five multi-view sequences, without numerical action traces, per-frame timing or a prediction-versus-execution legend.

evidence.location: PDF p. 15, Figure 7; p. 17, Figure 9; pp. 20–21, Figures 10–11 and captions
evidence.detail: Figures 7 and 9 visualize VGM outputs. Figures 10–11 pair predicted and ground-truth world-model video for Agilex-Aloha-2 and AC-One, supplying qualitative fidelity evidence rather than measured task success.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 8–9, Section 6, Conclusion and Limitations
evidence.detail: Future work includes improved unified architectures, more universal motion priors and latent-action learning from internet-scale general videos.
